title: wikicc
html:
wikicc

Compile a folder of Markdown documents into a self-contained, offline HTML reader you can double-click.

The compiled reader needs no server, no sibling files and no network: search the whole folder, read a document with syntax highlighting and Mermaid diagrams, follow the link graph between documents, and navigate long documents through their chapter outline.

Features

Reader

  • Search over titles, headings and body text, including CJK.
  • Link graph of the folder with zoom, pan and drag; clicking a node opens that document.
  • Chapter outline of the current document, following the section being read.
  • Chapter folding: an arrow beside a heading folds that chapter — and everything nested under it — down to its title, and unfolds it again. The arrows appear when the pointer is on a heading and stay out of the way otherwise; folding is never remembered, so every document opens whole. Following a link or an outline entry into a folded chapter reopens it.
  • Block references: a link to a chapter of another document previews that chapter on hover and opens it on click, and a link to a whole document previews that document on hover. A chapter that does not exist is reported as a broken reference and explained by the reader.
  • Tables: sorting and Excel-style per-column filtering. Filtering never shifts the column widths: they are measured at the last layout-affecting moment — the page loading, the window being resized — and pinned until the next one.
  • Code blocks: a button on every code block copies its text to the clipboard; inline code, diagrams and formulas are left alone.
  • Theme toggle (light/dark) and a layout that stays usable down to phone width.

Markdown support

  • GitHub-flavored Markdown: tables, task lists, strikethrough and footnotes.
  • Nested chapters with stable, Unicode-aware heading anchors, so CJK headings keep their text.
  • Chapter links: [label](path/to/doc.md#chapter) addresses one chapter of another document, [label](path/to/doc.md) addresses the document as a whole.
  • Images and other local assets: ![alt](path/to/image.png) is embedded content-addressed, and a destination containing spaces is accepted too.
  • Fenced code highlighting, done at build time.
  • Mermaid diagrams from a fence tagged mermaid.
  • Raw HTML inside Markdown, passed through unchanged. The input is trusted: there is no sanitizer, so do not compile untrusted documents.

Output formats

FormatArtifactAssets
single-html (default; one self-contained file)one index.htmlinlined into the page
html-dir (page plus an assets folder)index.html + assets/one file per unique resource
pages (static site for GitHub Pages)index.html + pages/ + search.json + assets/one file per unique resource

All three carry the same reader. Assets are content-addressed, so identical bytes are stored once no matter how many documents reference them.

  • single-html opens by double click, offline, from any directory, with no sibling files.
  • html-dir is smallest and can be copied, zipped or served statically as it is.
  • pages is a static site for an HTTP host such as GitHub Pages: the page carries the reader and a document manifest only, and each document's content is one JSON file under pages/ that the reader fetches when it navigates there. The search corpus is a separate search.json, fetched the first time the reader searches the whole site. Nothing but the shell and the manifest is downloaded up front, so first paint does not grow with the size of the folder. This format needs to be served over HTTP(S) — a browser refuses the fetches from a file:// page, and the reader says so when it finds itself there.

Publishing to GitHub Pages

pages output deploys as it is: hash routes need no server configuration, the file names are stable across builds (a cached page never points at a file a redeploy removed), and each fetch carries the content hash of the chunk it wants, so a browser that still holds a cached page refreshes its documents after a redeploy. The artifact works at the root of a domain and under a subpath alike:

wikicc path/to/docs --format pages -o site
git -C path/to/docs add site && git -C path/to/docs commit -m "Publish"
git -C path/to/docs subtree push --prefix site origin gh-pages

Offline and reproducibility

  • The shell formats fetch nothing at runtime: no CDN, no web font, no remote stylesheet. pages fetches only the files the build wrote next to the page — never a third-party origin.
  • The build itself never touches the network; the only network step is the one-time npm ci that installs the pinned front-end dependencies.
  • Two builds of the same input produce byte-identical artifacts, in every format.

Usage

Prerequisites and install

  • Rust 1.85 or newer (the crate uses edition 2024).
  • Node.js 22.12 or newer and npm — the reader is bundled at build time, and 22.12 is the floor of the diagram engine. Node is needed for the build and the quality tooling: build.rs runs the native esbuild executable of the @esbuild/<os>-<cpu> package directly, and the formatter and linter of the front-end sources are installed into the same node_modules.
npm ci                     # once, and again whenever package-lock.json changes
cargo build --release      # build.rs bundles the reader into the binary
cargo install --path .     # optional: put `wikicc` on PATH

The compiled binary and the generated HTML have no external dependencies.

Prebuilt binaries

The releases page carries the binaries CI builds for each tagged version, one archive per build system and architecture:

Build systemArchitectureArchiveBinary inside
Ubuntuamd64wikicc-ubuntu-amd64-v<version>-<sha>.tar.gzwikicc
Windowsamd64wikicc-windows-amd64-v<version>-<sha>.zipwikicc.exe

The archive name states the system it was built on rather than the kernel it runs on, so the same archive also tells you which CI image produced it. Unpack it anywhere and put the binary on PATH; nothing else has to be installed. The Ubuntu binary is statically linked against musl, so it runs on any distribution without a matching glibc, and the Windows executable links the C runtime statically, so it does not need the VC++ redistributable.

Command line

wikicc [OPTIONS] [INPUT_DIR]

  -o, --out <DIR>        Output directory [default: <INPUT_DIR>/dist]
      --format <FMT>     single-html | html-dir | pages [default: single-html]
      --title <TITLE>    Site title [default: input folder name]
      --strict[=<BOOL>]  Treat warnings as errors; --strict=false turns the gate off
      --home <DOC>       Document the reader opens first; overrides .wikicc.json
      --exclude <DIR>    Directory to keep out of the site; repeatable, overrides .wikicc.json
      --favicon <FILE>   Favicon file relative to the input folder; overrides
                         .wikicc.json [default: the wikicc logo]
      --force            Overwrite the output directory without confirmation
  -q, --quiet            Suppress the summary line
      --init-config [DIR]
                         Write a default .wikicc.json into DIR [default: the
                         current directory] and exit
  -h, --help             Print help
  -V, --version          Print version

wikicc path/to/docs                       # writes path/to/docs/dist/index.html
wikicc path/to/docs -o build --title "Handbook"
wikicc path/to/docs --format html-dir
wikicc path/to/docs --format pages        # a static site for GitHub Pages
wikicc path/to/docs --strict              # broken links fail the build
wikicc path/to/docs --home guide/intro.md # override the configured opening document
wikicc path/to/docs --exclude drafts      # override the configured exclusions
wikicc path/to/docs --favicon assets/icon.png
wikicc --init-config path/to/docs         # writes path/to/docs/.wikicc.json

A successful build prints a summary line and reports diagnostics on stderr; --quiet suppresses the summary only.

Output directory

  • A missing directory is created; an empty one is used as it is.
  • A directory holding a previous build is emptied and reused, so rebuilding needs no flags and leaves no stale files.
  • Any other non-empty directory requires --force.
  • The output directory cannot be the input folder, an ancestor of it, or the current working directory, and it is excluded from scanning.
  • Symlinks inside the output directory are removed as links, never followed.

Configuration file

A site can carry an optional .wikicc.json in the input folder root. The file is JSON and knows keys — the same settings the command line takes, so each of them can also be overridden by a flag:

KeyMeaning
homeDocument the reader opens at an empty or unknown address [default: the first document]
excludeDirectories whose entire subtrees stay out of the site [default: none]
outOutput directory [default: <INPUT_DIR>/dist]
formatsingle-html, html-dir or pages [default: single-html]
titleSite title [default: the input folder name]
faviconFavicon file relative to the input folder [default: the wikicc logo]
strictFail the build on warnings [default: false]

home is a document id — the path relative to the input folder, / separated, extension included — and a missing .md (or .markdown) suffix is completed, so "home": "intro" addresses intro.md. Explicit links are never redirected: the setting only decides what the opening page shows, and the sidebar, graph and search see the same document they always did.

exclude lists directories relative to the input folder; each pruned directory takes its documents and subfolders with it, so drafts and private notes never reach the payload, the search index or the link graph. Entries are normalized like home values — trimmed, \ read as /, a leading ./ and a trailing / dropped — and match exactly: "drafts" prunes the input folder's own drafts directory, not guide/drafts. The build reports how many directories were pruned as a note line.

out is resolved against the input folder — the directory the configuration file sits in — so a relative value builds to the same place no matter which working directory the build was started from. A command line --out keeps its own convention: relative to the working directory.

favicon is a file path relative to the input folder (\ is read as /, a leading ./ is dropped; an absolute path is taken as it is). Every page carries it as its <link rel="icon">: the icon travels through the same content-addressed asset system as the documents' images, inlined as a data URI by single-html and written to assets/ by the other two formats. Without the key the reader carries the wikicc logo, which is embedded into the executable at build time.

{
  "home": "guide/getting-started.md",
  "exclude": ["drafts", "archive/old"],
  "out": "site",
  "format": "pages",
  "title": "Handbook",
  "favicon": "assets/icon.png",
  "strict": false
}

Every value the file names is a default; an explicit flag wins.

  • --home replaces the configured home.
  • --exclude replaces the configured list entirely; repeat the flag for several directories.
  • --out, --format, --title and --favicon override their configured counterparts.
  • A bare --strict turns the gate on and --strict=false turns it off, whatever the file says.
  • --force and --quiet exist only on the command line; the file never asks for a destructive overwrite or a silent build.
  • A home that matches no document is a warning — the build still succeeds and the reader falls back to the first document; --strict turns it into a failure.
  • An exclude entry that escapes the input folder (..) or cannot match any directory (empty) fails the build for the same reason a broken home would, whatever the source it came from.
  • A favicon that is empty after normalization or escapes the input folder fails the build the same way, and a configured favicon file that cannot be read fails the build too: the icon is an explicit instruction, not something to silently replace with the default.
  • An unreadable or invalid file fails the build: a broken instruction must not be silently ignored.
  • Unknown keys warn, so a typo never silently changes nothing.
  • Every output format honours the settings, and a site without a .wikicc.json builds exactly the artifact it always did.

A starter file can be written with wikicc --init-config [DIR] (the current directory when the value is omitted). It writes the default content — every key unset:

{
  "home": null,
  "exclude": null,
  "out": null,
  "format": null,
  "title": null,
  "favicon": null,
  "strict": null
}
  • The target directory must already exist; a missing directory is rejected, not created.
  • An existing .wikicc.json is never overwritten — delete it first.
  • --init-config cannot be combined with an input directory.

Warnings and --strict

Broken links, missing assets, chapter anchors a document does not have and links that escape the input directory are warnings: the build still succeeds and the original destination is left untouched, so the reader can still show the link.

--strict turns warnings into a failure. The gate runs before anything is written, so a refused build neither creates an artifact nor empties a previous one.

Exit codes

CodeMeaning
0Success (possibly with warnings)
1Runtime failure: missing input, I/O error, --strict with warnings
2Usage error: invalid arguments

Documentation

  • CHANGELOG.md — what changed in each release.
  • docs/search.md — how the reader's search works, and the query syntax it understands.
  • docs/design.md — how wikicc is built.
  • docs/CONTRIBUTING.md — the development rules: the quality gates every commit has to pass, and the steps that regenerate the Windows icon.
  • tests/README.md — how the test suite is organised.

Development

See docs/CONTRIBUTING.md.

License

GPL-3.0-only. See LICENSE for the full text.

Node.js 22.12 or newer and npm — the reader is bundled at build time, and 22.12 is the floor of the diagram engine. Node is needed for the build and the quality tooling: build.rs runs the native esbuild executable of the @esbuild/<os>-<cpu> package directly, and the formatter and linter of the front-end sources are installed into the same node_modules. npm ci # once, and again whenever package-lock.json changes cargo build --release # build.rs bundles the reader into the binary cargo install --path . # optional: put `wikicc` on PATH The compiled binary and the generated HTML have no external dependencies. Prebuilt binaries The releases page carries the binaries CI builds for each tagged version, one archive per build system and architecture: Build system Architecture Archive Binary inside Ubuntu amd64 wikicc-ubuntu-amd64-v<version>-<sha>.tar.gz wikicc Windows amd64 wikicc-windows-amd64-v<version>-<sha>.zip wikicc.exe The archive name states the system it was built on rather than the kernel it runs on, so the same archive also tells you which CI image produced it. Unpack it anywhere and put the binary on PATH; nothing else has to be installed. The Ubuntu binary is statically linked against musl, so it runs on any distribution without a matching glibc, and the Windows executable links the C runtime statically, so it does not need the VC++ redistributable. Command line wikicc [OPTIONS] [INPUT_DIR] -o, --out <DIR> Output directory [default: <INPUT_DIR>/dist] --format <FMT> single-html | html-dir | pages [default: single-html] --title <TITLE> Site title [default: input folder name] --strict[=<BOOL>] Treat warnings as errors; --strict=false turns the gate off --home <DOC> Document the reader opens first; overrides .wikicc.json --exclude <DIR> Directory to keep out of the site; repeatable, overrides .wikicc.json --favicon <FILE> Favicon file relative to the input folder; overrides .wikicc.json [default: the wikicc logo] --force Overwrite the output directory without confirmation -q, --quiet Suppress the summary line --init-config [DIR] Write a default .wikicc.json into DIR [default: the current directory] and exit -h, --help Print help -V, --version Print version wikicc path/to/docs # writes path/to/docs/dist/index.html wikicc path/to/docs -o build --title "Handbook" wikicc path/to/docs --format html-dir wikicc path/to/docs --format pages # a static site for GitHub Pages wikicc path/to/docs --strict # broken links fail the build wikicc path/to/docs --home guide/intro.md # override the configured opening document wikicc path/to/docs --exclude drafts # override the configured exclusions wikicc path/to/docs --favicon assets/icon.png wikicc --init-config path/to/docs # writes path/to/docs/.wikicc.json A successful build prints a summary line and reports diagnostics on stderr; --quiet suppresses the summary only. Output directory A missing directory is created; an empty one is used as it is. A directory holding a previous build is emptied and reused, so rebuilding needs no flags and leaves no stale files. Any other non-empty directory requires --force. The output directory cannot be the input folder, an ancestor of it, or the current working directory, and it is excluded from scanning. Symlinks inside the output directory are removed as links, never followed. Configuration file A site can carry an optional .wikicc.json in the input folder root. The file is JSON and knows keys — the same settings the command line takes, so each of them can also be overridden by a flag: Key Meaning home Document the reader opens at an empty or unknown address [default: the first document] exclude Directories whose entire subtrees stay out of the site [default: none] out Output directory [default: <INPUT_DIR>/dist] format single-html, html-dir or pages [default: single-html] title Site title [default: the input folder name] favicon Favicon file relative to the input folder [default: the wikicc logo] strict Fail the build on warnings [default: false] home is a document id — the path relative to the input folder, / separated, extension included — and a missing .md (or .markdown) suffix is completed, so "home": "intro" addresses intro.md. Explicit links are never redirected: the setting only decides what the opening page shows, and the sidebar, graph and search see the same document they always did. exclude lists directories relative to the input folder; each pruned directory takes its documents and subfolders with it, so drafts and private notes never reach the payload, the search index or the link graph. Entries are normalized like home values — trimmed, \ read as /, a leading ./ and a trailing / dropped — and match exactly: "drafts" prunes the input folder's own drafts directory, not guide/drafts. The build reports how many directories were pruned as a note line. out is resolved against the input folder — the directory the configuration file sits in — so a relative value builds to the same place no matter which working directory the build was started from. A command line --out keeps its own convention: relative to the working directory. favicon is a file path relative to the input folder (\ is read as /, a leading ./ is dropped; an absolute path is taken as it is). Every page carries it as its <link rel="icon">: the icon travels through the same content-addressed asset system as the documents' images, inlined as a data URI by single-html and written to assets/ by the other two formats. Without the key the reader carries the wikicc logo, which is embedded into the executable at build time. { "home": "guide/getting-started.md", "exclude": ["drafts", "archive/old"], "out": "site", "format": "pages", "title": "Handbook", "favicon": "assets/icon.png", "strict": false } Every value the file names is a default; an explicit flag wins. --home replaces the configured home. --exclude replaces the configured list entirely; repeat the flag for several directories. --out, --format, --title and --favicon override their configured counterparts. A bare --strict turns the gate on and --strict=false turns it off, whatever the file says. --force and --quiet exist only on the command line; the file never asks for a destructive overwrite or a silent build. A home that matches no document is a warning — the build still succeeds and the reader falls back to the first document; --strict turns it into a failure. An exclude entry that escapes the input folder (..) or cannot match any directory (empty) fails the build for the same reason a broken home would, whatever the source it came from. A favicon that is empty after normalization or escapes the input folder fails the build the same way, and a configured favicon file that cannot be read fails the build too: the icon is an explicit instruction, not something to silently replace with the default. An unreadable or invalid file fails the build: a broken instruction must not be silently ignored. Unknown keys warn, so a typo never silently changes nothing. Every output format honours the settings, and a site without a .wikicc.json builds exactly the artifact it always did. A starter file can be written with wikicc --init-config [DIR] (the current directory when the value is omitted). It writes the default content — every key unset: { "home": null, "exclude": null, "out": null, "format": null, "title": null, "favicon": null, "strict": null } The target directory must already exist; a missing directory is rejected, not created. An existing .wikicc.json is never overwritten — delete it first. --init-config cannot be combined with an input directory. Warnings and --strict Broken links, missing assets, chapter anchors a document does not have and links that escape the input directory are warnings: the build still succeeds and the original destination is left untouched, so the reader can still show the link. --strict turns warnings into a failure. The gate runs before anything is written, so a refused build neither creates an artifact nor empties a previous one. Exit codes Code Meaning 0 Success (possibly with warnings) 1 Runtime failure: missing input, I/O error, --strict with warnings 2 Usage error: invalid arguments Documentation CHANGELOG.md — what changed in each release. docs/search.md — how the reader's search works, and the query syntax it understands. docs/design.md — how wikicc is built. docs/CONTRIBUTING.md — the development rules: the quality gates every commit has to pass, and the steps that regenerate the Windows icon. tests/README.md — how the test suite is organised.
